title: The Riverside Ballroom in Phoenix and 'chicken scratch' music
summary: He describes dancers at the Riverside Ballroom, the origin of the name 'chicken scratch', and playing with local bands around Arizona.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: I want to go back a little bit to when you were in Phoenix. You said you played a place called the Riverside.

And there were dances that were held there? Who were some of the people who came to these dances. I mean, I know they were local people certainly. Were they whites, blacks, were they people from Indian communities?
All mixed and I want to tell you that I'm proud to say that some Pimas had some real great, modern dancers. They had the rhythm, too.
They were doing some of the popular dances of the time, like the Lindy Hop, the Black Bottom?
How about some of this music that is indigenous to that area that has come to be called 'chicken scratch?' Was that starting around that time?
No, there was no 'chicken scratch' in those days, but the 'chicken scratch' music that you

brought over here that I listened to the other day, it reminded me of the Mexican influence in Arizona. I think the Indians adopted the Mexican style of dancing and that's where the "chicken scratch" comes from. Now all over the reservations in Arizona they have this "chicken scratch" music.

Do you know why they call it that, "chicken scratch," is because where they have the dances invariably the dances are held out there where there was no dance floor, just out on the dirt, on the earth and when you dance that dance you stir up a lot of dust. That's why they call it chickens dancing, "chicken scratch."

Well, did the bands come through say every weekend, every week for these dances or were they local orchestras that sometimes performed, and did you get a chance to perform in the Phoenix area or in Arizona while you were just sort of, you know, between the time that you got there from California and the time you went on with Eli Rice?
Well, I did happen to join local bands and play with them, we played all over the state,

like in Tucson, we'd go to Tucson to play something and then come back and -- I played with both black bands and a Mexican band and I made my little bread that way, but I couldn't exist like that. I wanted to get to New York, and instead of going to New York I got stranded in Monroe.
